bull.b: Large, durable Phase III data (nearly 600 in Part B, >1,000 across program) provide a durable clinical differentiation. Sustained single- and retreatment responses and tolerability strengthen label claims, support payer conversations and lower execution risk for commercialization over the next 2–6 months.

A rolling NDA and the Commissioner's National Priority Voucher materially shorten regulatory timelines if used, reducing time-to-market uncertainty. This structural regulatory advantage compresses the period of execution risk and supports earlier revenue potential and planning stability for launch activities.

Post-financing runway into 2028 plus experienced commercial hires materially improves probability of an organized launch. Availability of capital and a built-out commercial organization reduces short-term financing pressure and increases the odds of effective site onboarding and payer engagement during initial market entry.

bear.t: Persistent pre-revenue losses and cash burn
bear.b: The company remains pre-revenue with deep, recurrent operating and free cash flow deficits, creating structural dependence on external financing until commercial revenues materialize. Persistent cash burn elevates dilution and execution risk and constrains flexibility during the critical launch and reimbursement periods.

Category III tracking codes provide limited, temporary reimbursement certainty; progressing to Category I and achieving durable RVU valuation requires RUC/AMA work, real-world evidence and committee timing. This structural reimbursement gap can constrain physician economics and slow uptake even after approval.

Sequencing between FDA advisory processes, DEA rescheduling and REMS design could add months or operational complexity to launch. Open REMS/staffing requirements and DEA timing are structural execution risks that affect site readiness, training needs and early patient access even with an accelerated review mechanism.
